messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Cody Marsh is a 39-year-old divorced construction worker who presented for an initial psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 73, indicating severe post-traumatic stress. He is broad-shouldered and quietly spoken, choosing his words with the careful economy of a man who has learned that saying too much costs something. He was referred through his union's employee assistance program after a supervisor noticed a pattern of absences and what colleagues described as episodes of "zoning out" on the worksite.

Approximately fourteen months before this intake, Cody was working a commercial renovation job when a co-worker and friend of seven years, a man named Dale, fell from unsecured scaffolding three floors above street level. Cody was directly below, mixing compound, when the structure gave way. He watched Dale fall and land on the concrete a few metres away. What followed — the sound, the smell of blood and dust and something he has never been able to name, the acrid taste that coated his mouth in the moments he knelt beside Dale screaming for help — became the sensory architecture of a memory that has refused to stay in the past. Dale survived but sustained catastrophic injuries. Cody walked away without a scratch, a fact that has never felt like luck to him.

In the weeks after the accident, Cody found that the memory returned not as a narrative he could recount but as a cascade of images — a freeze-frame of Dale's body mid-fall, the colour of the concrete, the particular angle of light that afternoon. These pictures arrived without warning, and with them came the smell, something metallic and chemical that he cannot always locate in the external world but that arrives with full conviction. More disturbing still, there are moments when he can taste what he tasted that day — a specific, visceral sensation that arrives in his mouth and makes him feel that the afternoon on the scaffold is happening now rather than a year ago.

Cody had come to believe, in the months that followed, that the world he thought he understood — one in which a man who works carefully and looks out for his crew can keep the people around him safe — no longer existed. He was certain that bad things would continue to happen regardless of anything he did or did not do, and he had arrived at a quiet, settled conviction that he was inadequate: not merely that he had failed Dale in that specific moment, but that inadequacy was something constitutive of him, a fixed feature rather than a circumstance.

What frightened him most was the anger. In the days after the accident Cody had felt a rage so large it seemed dangerous to him, and he made a decision — not quite conscious, but firm — that he would never allow himself to feel or express it. He became, by his own account, very still. Colleagues noticed he no longer argued on the site, no longer pushed back when work was unsafe. The man who had once been the loudest voice in a safety meeting now signed off on conditions he would previously have refused. This change had a concrete professional consequence: three months ago, a junior worker on his crew was injured when Cody failed to flag a hazard he had seen and said nothing about.

In the evenings, Cody drove to a casino forty minutes from his apartment. He was clear-eyed about what he was doing there — it was not about winning. The noise and the lights and the specific quality of suspense at the table gave him something to feel that was not the images and not the stillness. On the nights he could not bring himself to drive, he found ways to go somewhere else internally, to blank out, to leave his body sitting in the chair while he went somewhere that had no sensory texture at all.

His divorce had been finalised six months before the accident, and he now lived alone. There was no one at home to notice when he returned at two in the morning, and no one to remark on the money disappearing from his account. What finally brought him in was the incident with the junior worker — not guilt exactly, but a recognition that something was happening to him that he could no longer manage alone. He arrived at the intake hoping, with considerable scepticism, that someone might be able to tell him whether the person he used to be was recoverable, or whether that man had also fallen that afternoon on the scaffold.
